subject: 🌎 Brave new world
body_text:
96 
Plus: The worst week | Monday, November 23, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Nov 23, 2026
 
 
 🌅 Welcome back to a thankfully short week . It's a whole new markets picture out there. More on that below.

 This morning, U.S. stock futures are up sharply — and Anthropic and Nvidia are both up in premarket trading — after last week's ugly selloff. Asian markets were down overnight, battered by the AI trade. Let's get moving. In 842 words, a 3-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: A new era for the AI trade
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 
 
 Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios


 
   
 
 The AI trade has entered uncharted territory as stocks limp to the end of an astonishing month.

 The big picture: An important new reality for AI emerged in the just concluded third-quarter earnings season that has been overshadowed by the midterm elections, Jensen Huang and the Anthropic IPO. 

 Zoom in: Wall Street analysts covering the hyperscalers didn't ratchet up forecasts for further capital investment by Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle — the biggest spenders of the AI data center boom.

 That's a change from recent trends, seen in the chart below, where tech giants regularly announced shocking amounts of planned AI investment as part of quarterly results. Those announcements would lead Wall Street analysts to increase their estimates, and the capex line would spike up and to the right. Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Reality check: This flatlining trend is huge. 

 That wave of hyperscaler investment into data centers is also the source of giant profits that other companies — construction and engineering firms, merchant power providers, fiber-optic cable makers and, of course, makers of chips and memory devices — have been raking in from the boom. The AI investment gravy train has driven levels of S&P 500 earnings growth and overall corporate profitability to remarkably high levels. Threat level: Slower capex will curb profits for the "picks-and-shovels" AI stocks that delivered some of the most astonishing gains of the AI boom.

 That's not necessarily a disaster: Analysts are expecting a more-than-respectable 16.4% increase in earnings for the S&P 500 next year. But it's clearly a sharp slowdown from earnings-per-share growth of nearly 35% that Wall Street thinks we'll end up with in 2026. What they're saying: "We think the nature of the market environment is shifting a bit away from this sort of constantly higher capex numbers," David Lefkowitz, head of U.S. equities at UBS Global Wealth Management, told Axios last week, adding: "We need to see the monetization at the AI layer, because that's ultimately who's paying for all this capex."

 What we're watching: As Lefkowitz says, we're watching for clear, conclusive proof that there's serious money to be made from AI — aside from selling equipment used to build data centers. We haven't seen it yet. 

 The bottom line: Slowing future earnings expectations, expected Federal Reserve interest rate hikes and the chance of increased AI regulation have the market on edge.

2. The month that changed the market
 
   
 
 Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios October was supposed to be spooky season, but November has been the real nightmare for investors.

 By the numbers: The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 11.1% since Nov. 1. 

 The closely watched SOX semiconductor index, which tracks many of the high-flying chip stocks, is off 21.2% over that same period. Nvidia, the premier stock of the AI trade, is down a shocking 38.4% this month. The stock closed at $125.53 on Friday. In May, it was trading at more than $220. The big picture: Both the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, are now in correction territory — meaning down more than 10% from their most recent highs.

 The latest: Last week was the worst for the S&P 500 since President Trump's "Liberation Day" in April 2025.

 Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Reality check: The S&P 500 is still up for the year, albeit just 0.8%.

 What to watch: "Wall Street is at risk of its first down year since 2022, which also featured a midterm election and Fed rate hikes," José Torres, senior economist at Interactive Brokers, wrote in a note Friday afternoon. 

 Catch up quick: AI fever was already starting to break coming into November, and then three developments appear to have crushed the vibes.

 Across the country, Americans voted overwhelmingly for AI-skeptical candidates and ballot measures constraining data center construction, and Trump — a huge AI booster — was politically weakened by historic Democratic gains in the midterms. Huang, who helped fuel the AI infrastructure boom by extending a range of unorthodox financial lifelines to smaller, heavily indebted AI players, resigned as Nvidia CEO in disgrace, rocking a pillar of the industry. AI lab Anthropic listed its shares in the biggest offering of all time, but the widely watched milestone failed to lift investor sentiment on tech, and shares continued to tumble. Our thought bubble: In times like these, it's best to avoid checking your 401(k), especially if retirement is a long way away.
